items.readable_text:
Content:
Suppose that we want to solve the following quadratic equation:
[MATH: (x+1)^2 = 4.]

Content:
Notice that the left-hand side is a perfect square and the right-hand side is a constant:

Content:
[MATH: \underbrace{(x+1)^2}_{\large\color{blue}\textrm{perfect square}} = \overbrace{\!\!\!\!\!4\!\!\!\!\!}^{\large\color{red}\textrm{constant}} \!\!\!\!\!]
In this case, we can solve the equation using the square root method. First, we take the square root of both sides:
[MATH: (x + 1)^{2}|= 4; sqrt((x + 1)^{2})|= sqrt(4);|x + 1||= 2]

Content:
Then, we solve the resulting absolute value equation:
[MATH: |x + 1||= 2; x + 1|= ± 2; x|= − 1 ± 2]

Content:
Finally, we simplify the two solutions:

Content:
[MATH: x|= − 1 + 2 = 1; x|= − 1 − 2 = − 3]

Content:
Therefore, the solutions are [MATH: x=-3] and [MATH: x=1.]

items.title: Equations Where the Perfect Square Is Not Isolated

sections.normalized_html:
First, we isolate the perfect square:

[MATH: − 2(3x − 6)^{2} + 1|= − 9; − 2(3x − 6)^{2}|= − 10; (3x − 6)^{2}|= 5]

Then, we solve the equation using the square root method:

[MATH: sqrt((3x − 6)^{2})|= sqrt(5);|3x − 6||= sqrt(5); 3x − 6|= ± sqrt(5); 3x|= 6 ± sqrt(5); x|= (6 ± sqrt(5))/(3); x|= (6)/(3) ± (sqrt(5))/(3); x|= 2 ± (sqrt(5))/(3)]

The two solutions are

[MATH: x= 2 + \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{3}\quad \textrm{and}\quad x= 2 - \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{3}.]

However, because these solutions cannot be simplified any further, we will keep the "[MATH: \pm]" symbol in our final answer. So our final answer is

[MATH: x = 2 \pm \dfrac{\sqrt{5}}{3}.]

sections.normalized_html:
First, notice that the left-hand side is a perfect square. It just needs to be factored:

[MATH: t^{2} − 10t + 25|= 121; t^{2} − 2 ⋅ 5 ⋅ t + 5^{2}|= 121; (t − 5)^{2}|= 121]

From here, we solve the equation using the square root method: [MATH: sqrt((t − 5)^{2})|= sqrt(121);|t − 5||= 11; t − 5|= ± 11; t|= 5 ± 11]

Next, we simplify the two solutions:

[MATH: t|= 5 + 11 = 16; t|= 5 − 11 = − 6]

Therefore, the solutions are [MATH: t=-6] and [MATH: t=16.]

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

Content:
Suppose that we want to solve the following quadratic equation:
[MATH: (x+1)^2 = 4.]

Content:
Notice that the left-hand side is a perfect square and the right-hand side is a constant:

Content:
[MATH: \underbrace{(x+1)^2}_{\large\color{blue}\textrm{perfect square}} = \overbrace{\!\!\!\!\!4\!\!\!\!\!}^{\large\color{red}\textrm{constant}} \!\!\!\!\!]
In this case, we can solve the equation using the square root method. First, we take the square root of both sides:
[MATH: (x + 1)^{2}|= 4; sqrt((x + 1)^{2})|= sqrt(4);|x + 1||= 2]

Content:
Then, we solve the resulting absolute value equation:
[MATH: |x + 1||= 2; x + 1|= ± 2; x|= − 1 ± 2]

Content:
Finally, we simplify the two solutions:

Content:
[MATH: x|= − 1 + 2 = 1; x|= − 1 − 2 = − 3]

Content:
Therefore, the solutions are [MATH: x=-3] and [MATH: x=1.]

---

Item 2 — Example: Equations Where the Perfect Square is Isolated

Example Prompt:
Solve [MATH: (3y +2)^2 = 4.]

Content:

Explanation:
We solve the equation using the square root method:

[MATH: (3y + 2)^{2}|= 4; sqrt((3y + 2)^{2})|= sqrt(4);|3y + 2||= 2; 3y + 2|= ± 2; 3y|= − 2 ± 2; y|= (− 2 ± 2)/(3)]

Next, we simplify the two solutions:

[MATH: y|= (− 2 + 2)/(3) = 0; y|= (− 2 − 2)/(3) = − (4)/(3)]

Therefore, the solutions are [MATH: y=-\dfrac{4}{3}] and [MATH: y=0.]
